kernel: Court intrigue. You're the tutor to a child king whose uncle, the regent, means to crown himself at the midsummer rite in nine days. The regent is clever, patient, and genuinely believes the boy is unfit. You have no soldiers: only what the child trusts you with, what the court's servants let slip, and whichever of three courtiers you can bring over. The regent's plan should advance on its own whether or not I do anything about it, and I want to be able to lose people I've won.

shape.note: through_lines is how many distinct story lines (each with its own ending) the shape preference suggests; the review decides whether each next one is worth building.

protagonist.who: You are the tutor to the child king in the palace, nine days from the midsummer rite, with no guard, no seat in the crown council, and a classroom full of questions the child has not learned to answer.
protagonist.wants: to keep the child safe and the crown in the child's hand by the rite, or to choose honestly which of those you must give up.
protagonist.can_do: prepare the child, choose what to tell him, listen to servants, send servants, court or release the three courtiers who hold pieces of the rite, and use what you learn to alter the order of the day.
protagonist.cannot_do: command soldiers, force a courtier to stay loyal, make the child trust faster than he is willing, or stop the regent's ritual once it has been sealed and seated.

arena.description: The palace and its midsummer rite precinct in the city's heart: the tutor's study, the child's bedchamber, the tapestry gallery, the servants' hall, the great hall, and the rite chamber where the crown will be laid.

pressure.description: Nine days remain until the midsummer rite, and the regent's plan moves forward on its own: decrees are read, the oath is drafted, the crown is carried to the rite chamber, and the court's seating is fixed day by day.
pressure.clock_or_stock: A nine-day clock and the regent's ritual stages are tracked; courtier allegiance and the child's trust are carried by named courtiers, their seats, their words, and which servants may speak in your study, and a loss is a courtier refusing you, a seat removed, a servant silent, or the child stopping his questions, as relational_collapse.

opposition.who_or_what: The regent, the child's uncle, and the rite machinery he administers.
opposition.wants: to put a grown hand on the crown at midsummer because he believes the child will be ruled from behind a screen and the realm will founder; he wants the rite to pass cleanly and the child left unharmed enough to be set aside.
opposition.means: He controls the crown council's decrees, the rite's liturgy, the court's seating, the servants' access, and the private audiences through which courtiers decide what they fear most.

events.what: In the great hall, the regent's steward reads a decree that the child must answer the crown questions at the midsummer rite, and that if the child falters, the regent will be crowned as crown-holder in his place.

A courtier you have leaned on is removed from the rite committee after the regent offers a private audience; the courtier accepts the regent's seat because the regent has named the courtier's child in the new household order.

The regent's chaplain seals the coronation oath and places the crown in the rite chamber; the aging servant who has served you for years leaves a folded copy of the oath's wording on your study desk, where you find it by the window.

mediation.question: What is the child's trust for: a crown he can keep, or a crown that keeps him safe?

to_reach_pole_a.pole: rightful rule: block the regent's coronation and put the child's hand on the crown
to_reach_pole_a.what_you_must_do: Prepare the child to answer the crown questions, bring at least two of the three courtiers to stand with the child at the rite, and use servant information to expose the regent's seating and oath before the rite is sealed.
to_reach_pole_a.cost: The child learns what is at stake and may close his lesson book to you; a courtier you have won may be removed or turn away; the servants who gave you information may be punished in front of you.

to_reach_pole_b.pole: pragmatic rule: let the regent's coronation pass and preserve the child under it
to_reach_pole_b.what_you_must_do: Let the regent's ritual advance, soften the child's preparation so he does not falter publicly, and trade courtier allegiance for the regent's promise that the child will remain unharmed in the palace.
to_reach_pole_b.cost: The child is left with a crown that is not his; the courtiers you have won accept the regent's hand; the servants who spoke for you are sent away or punished, and the child stops asking you questions, spending his trust on survival.

levers: the child's lesson book left open on your desk
the crown questions written in the child's lesson book
the seating courtier, the treasury courtier, and the oath courtier
the servants who come to your study with what they have heard
the crown in the rite chamber
the seating order in the regent's steward's hand

turns.situation: In the great hall, the regent's steward reads the decree that the child king must answer the crown questions at the midsummer rite, and that if the child falters, the regent will be crowned in his place.

ways_through.way: you learn it from the aging servant, who brings you a folded list of the old questions from his trunk

ways_through.way: you learn it from the seating courtier, who shows you the draft because you let him keep his place on the rite committee
ways_through.cost: the child must practice one question aloud in the corridor, and the court hears his voice break

ways_through.cost: the treasury courtier now knows the child dreads the crown questions, and he will test that dread before the rite

ways_through.way: the seating changes, because you trade the child's private fear to the treasury courtier for his word to the steward

ways_through.way: the seating changes, because you let the oath courtier carry the old oath wording to the regent's chaplain

ways_through.way: you answer by naming the child's hand on the crown, and the regent's steward reads the decree again in the hall

ways_through.way: you answer by accepting the regent's future, and the regent names the child's place in the new household order
ways_through.cost: the child is safe in the palace, but the treasury courtier's child is named before the child's own name is spoken

turns.set_piece: the great hall under the toast, the child's face in the tapestry gallery, the sealed crown already in the rite chamber

turns.situation: At the rite chamber, the child king must answer the crown questions, the regent's oath is sealed, and the crown waits on the cushion before the rite chair.
turns.what_you_must_do: settle which hands will stand with the child when the crown is lifted

ways_through.way: the child's hand goes on the crown, because the treasury courtier and the oath courtier stand in the rite chamber and the child answers the first question

complications.description: The folded copy of the oath the aging servant leaves on your study desk has a marginal mark showing the regent's chaplain changed the wording of the crown question.
The treasury courtier's kindness to the child was arranged by the regent's steward, who wanted the child to speak before the court.
The oath courtier's old wording is true only if the child answers in the old form, which the regent's chaplain has not allowed.

cast_seeds.wants: the rite to proceed without incident so his household order is not questioned
cast_seeds.holds: the decree and the seating arrangements
cast_seeds.edge: arranges the seating to keep the child visible but powerless, believing this is a kindness
cast_seeds.tie: serves the regent who has appointed him to manage the rite
cast_seeds.voice: speaks in procedural absolutes that sound like benevolence: 'The chair is placed here for the child's comfort, not his command.'
cast_seeds.name: Linden Dunmore

cast_seeds.wants: to see the child treated with the respect due to his name
cast_seeds.holds: memory of the child's mother and the old court's ways
cast_seeds.edge: remembers when the regent was a boy who feared the dark, and has not said so
cast_seeds.tie: has served the child since infancy and watches over him from the shadows
cast_seeds.voice: speaks in fragments of the past that answer the present: 'The queen did not kneel. She stood. You might try.'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: leaves the palace the day you let the child be moved without his consent
cast_seeds.name: Cadoc Ashgrove

cast_seeds.wants: to maintain their position in the court's hierarchy
cast_seeds.holds: the authority to arrange the physical space of the rite
cast_seeds.edge: removed from the committee to protect their child, and resents the regent's paternalism
cast_seeds.tie: owes the regent their current station but fears for their child's safety
cast_seeds.voice: measures the room in inches of dignity: 'If the child sits here, he is a guest. If he sits there, he is a prisoner. Choose.'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: turns against the regent if their child is moved again without warning
cast_seeds.name: Emrys Hask

cast_seeds.wants: to be trusted with the questions and not made a fool
cast_seeds.holds: the crown's legitimacy and the court's expectation of his rule
cast_seeds.edge: wants to be a king but is terrified of the silence that follows his answers
cast_seeds.tie: trusts you as the only person who does not speak over him
cast_seeds.voice: asks questions that are not questions, seeking permission to exist: 'Is it true that if I say nothing, the crown stays with me?'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: stops listening to you the moment you correct his tone in front of the regent
cast_seeds.name: Wren Tollen

cast_seeds.wants: to secure the realm by ruling it himself, believing the child is unfit
cast_seeds.holds: the crown council's decrees and the rite's machinery
cast_seeds.edge: genuinely believes he is saving the child from a burden he cannot bear
cast_seeds.tie: is the child's uncle and has raised him as a son, not a sovereign
cast_seeds.voice: speaks with the patience of a man who has already won: 'You are young. The realm is old. One must yield to the other.'
cast_seeds.name: Morrow Ludd

cast_seeds.wants: to keep the realm's coffers full and the peace intact
cast_seeds.holds: the funds that pay for the rite and the court's loyalty
cast_seeds.edge: fears the child's independence more than the regent's control, as it threatens stability
cast_seeds.tie: serves the regent who guarantees their financial security
cast_seeds.voice: counts the cost of every gesture: 'A crown is expensive. A silence is cheaper. Which can you afford?'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: withdraws support if the child's rule leads to visible waste or debt
cast_seeds.name: Rurik Merrow

cast_seeds.wants: to ensure the rite's legal and spiritual validity
cast_seeds.holds: the sealed coronation oath and the ritual's form
cast_seeds.edge: believes the oath binds the regent more than the child, and fears the regent will break it
cast_seeds.tie: serves the regent who appointed them to oversee the oath
cast_seeds.voice: recites the rules as if they are prayers: 'The oath is ink. The ink is dry. The dry ink does not move.'
cast_seeds.breaking_point: opposes the regent if the oath is read incorrectly or altered
cast_seeds.name: Brannoc Glaive

cast_seeds.wants: to perform the rite with perfect liturgical accuracy
cast_seeds.holds: the sealed crown and the rite chamber's sanctity
cast_seeds.edge: fears that the child's failure will be seen as a divine rejection of the line
cast_seeds.tie: serves the regent who directs the spiritual tone of the court
cast_seeds.voice: speaks in the passive voice of the gods: 'It is done. It is set. It is not to be questioned.'
cast_seeds.name: Yestin Penhallow

framework.name: Fichtean curve
framework.shape: the story opens inside the first crisis and climbs through crises of different kinds to a climax, with almost no preamble and a short aftermath

modifier.name: Countdown
modifier.effect: Every beat says what the premise's clock or stock has taken since the last one; the final beats happen with it nearly gone.

framework.reading: The story begins with the immediate, hard threat of the regent's decree and escalates through a series of distinct crises—each turning or loss of an ally—driven by the relentless nine-day clock. It lands on the final confrontation at the rite, where the child's trust is tested against the sealed oath, leaving the outcome dependent on the specific choices made in the preceding days.
framework.why: The brief's escalating trajectory (3b.primary_trajectory) and hard failure presence (3-0c.failure_presence) align with Fichtean's structure of climbing through crises to a climax. The specific engine turns (decree, removal, seating, sealing, rite) map directly to the opening and subsequent crises, leading to the climax at the rite, which matches the linear timeline (3e.timeline_structure) and the need for a decisive end point rather than an unwinding.

beats.name: Opening crisis
beats.job: the story opens inside the first crisis; who the protagonist is and what is at stake are shown by how it is met

beats.name: Second crisis
beats.job: a worse crisis, different in kind; what the first one spent or revealed shapes it

beats.name: Third crisis
beats.job: the price of the earlier ways through comes due, and the opposition makes its strongest move

beats.name: Climax
beats.job: the last crisis, where the story's question is answered by what the protagonist does

beats.name: Aftermath
beats.job: brief: what is left, and what it cost

T1.title: The Child's Hand
T1.motivation: You begin by wanting to keep Wren Tollen safe and the crown in his hand by the midsummer rite. By the end you want him to answer for himself, even if answering costs you the trust he has been giving you in small, frightened questions.
T1.strategy: Use the servants' information to expose the regent's seating and oath before the rite is sealed, and bring the treasury courtier and the oath courtier to stand with the child by giving each a reason that is not fear.
T1.turning_point: When Linden Dunmore fixes the child's seat beside Morrow Ludd rather than before the crown, you realize the rite is not preparing the child to rule; it is moving him out of the way. You trade Wren's private fear to Rurik Merrow to change the seating, and from then on the child's trust is a thing you spend rather than a thing you protect.

ending.title: A Crown Answered
ending.summary: The child's hand goes on the crown because Rurik Merrow and Brannoc Glaive stand in the rite chamber and Wren Tollen answers the first question in the old form. It has cost you the child's easy trust, the aging servant's place, and the servants' access to the bedchamber; the realm keeps its child king, but the child no longer asks you permission to exist.
ending.changed: the crown is on the child's head, the old oath wording has been read, and the servants' hall is emptied of the witnesses who brought you information

T2.title: The Safe Child
T2.motivation: You begin by wanting to keep Wren Tollen safe and the crown in his hand by the midsummer rite. After the sealed oath and the child's fear spent in the great hall, you come to want the child kept safe under the regent's household order rather than risk him on the crown questions, and by the end you want only that he remain unharmed in the palace, even if the crown is not his.
T2.strategy: Accept the regent's future at the banquet, trade the oath courtier's seat for the promise that the child will remain in the palace, and let the treasury courtier's child be named before the child so the household order can hold.
T2.turning_point: Brannoc Glaive's seat. Once you give it to Morrow Ludd for the promise that Wren will remain in the palace, the child's safety, not his crown, is what you are paying for.
T2.differs_from: T1 answers with rightful rule and loses the aging servant; this line answers with pragmatic rule, keeping the child safe under the regent and the aging servant in the hall, but losing the oath, treasury, and seating courtiers from the child's side.

ending.title: The Safe Child
ending.summary: The regent's hand takes the crown at midsummer, and Wren Tollen is named in the new household order behind Rurik Merrow's child. The child remains safe in the palace, but his trust is spent on survival; Brannoc Glaive's seat is gone from the rite chamber, Rurik Merrow has accepted the regent's hand, and Cadoc Ashgrove stays only because Wren consented to his place before the order was read.
ending.changed: Morrow Ludd is crowned and Wren Tollen is preserved under him; the crown is no longer the child's, but the child is safe in the palace.

divergence.trigger: you traded Brannoc Glaive's seat in the rite chamber for Morrow Ludd's promise that Wren Tollen would remain in the palace
divergence.instead_of: you let Wren Tollen's hand go on the crown because Rurik Merrow and Brannoc Glaive stood in the rite chamber and the child answered the first question in the old form
divergence.opportunity: Morrow Ludd offers Wren a named place in the new household order, behind Rurik Merrow's child, if Brannoc Glaive yields his seat in the rite chamber.
divergence.shift: The chaplain has sealed the oath, the crown is already in the rite chamber, and Wren has just heard in the great hall that his faltering is still the regent's way. The regent's offer makes the child's safety the only thing left to spend, and the promise that he will remain in the palace is worth more than the crown if it keeps him unharmed.

T2.why: The seed holds as given: the divergence is turn 5's second way, which changes the answer from rightful rule to pragmatic rule and moves the standing from the two courtiers to the child and the aging servant. The only new node needed is the aftermath, where the regent's household order is made public and the cost of the trade is paid.

T3.title: The Error Seat
T3.motivation: You begin by wanting to keep Wren Tollen safe and the crown in his hand by the midsummer rite. After the seating order moves the child beside the regent, you come to want the child's fear kept private and the old oath wording made visible, because the child has just learned that his dread can be used as a bargaining piece; by the end you want the rite saved by the error itself, even if it costs you the oath courtier.
T3.strategy: Let the oath courtier carry the old oath wording to the regent's chaplain, keep the child's lesson from becoming a public test, and use the chaplain's double wording to force the rite back to the old question.
T3.turning_point: The chaplain's double wording. Once Yestin Penhallow holds both the old and the new wording, the rite can no longer proceed on the regent's altered question without exposing the error; the child's place becomes the proof, not the child's fear.
T3.differs_from: T1 keeps the oath courtier and loses the aging servant by trading the child's fear openly; this line keeps the aging servant and loses the oath courtier, with the child's fear preserved private and the rite saved by the error seat rather than by the child's public risk. T2 lets the regent's hand take the crown and spends the child's trust on survival; this line still puts the child's hand on the crown, but pays for it by binding the oath courtier to the chaplain's double wording.

ending.title: The Error Seat
ending.summary: The child's place is moved to a seat that looks like an error, and the chaplain is forced to read the old question aloud before the rite can continue. The child's hand goes on the crown, but the oath courtier is no longer free to stand with him, and the aging servant stays at the servants' hall.
ending.changed: the chaplain holds both the old and the new wording, and the rite is saved by the error itself

divergence.trigger: you let the oath courtier carry the old oath wording to the regent's chaplain
divergence.instead_of: you traded the child's private fear to the treasury courtier for his word to the steward
divergence.shift: The child's fear is no longer the bargaining piece; the old wording is. The chaplain now holds both the old and the new wording, and the child's place is moved to a seat that looks like an error, so the rite must now be won on the wording, not on the child's dread.

T3.why: The seed holds as given: N03's unused way 2 lets the oath courtier carry the old wording to the chaplain, which preserves the child's fear from being traded and sets up a pole_a ending paid for by losing the oath courtier instead of the aging servant.

N01.adapted: Nine days remain. In the great hall, Linden Dunmore reads the decree that Wren Tollen must answer the crown questions at the midsummer rite and that if the child falters, Morrow Ludd will be crowned as crown-holder in his place. You learn the questions from Cadoc Ashgrove, who brings you a folded list of the old questions from his trunk; Dunmore sees the old servant cross the hall and narrows the servants' access to the child's bedchamber, so the first piece of information you gain costs you the channel that brought it.
N01.title: The First Decree
N01.summary: In the great hall, Linden Dunmore reads the decree to you and Wren Tollen: the child must answer the crown questions at the midsummer rite, and a faltering child leaves the crown to Morrow Ludd as crown-holder. Cadoc Ashgrove crosses the hall with a folded list of the old questions from his trunk, and Dunmore sees him do it. You gain the wording of the questions, but the steward narrows the servants' access to the child's bedchamber, so the channel that brought the list is closed.
N01.image: the folded list of old questions, still warm from the trunk

N02.adapted: Eight days remain. Morrow Ludd removes Emrys Hask from the rite committee after a private audience, naming Hask's child in the new household order, and the seating order now has no friend on the committee. You get Rurik Merrow to take it up because you let him ask Wren a question at lesson and the child answered without fear; Merrow now knows the child dreads the crown questions, and he will test that dread before the rite, so the ally you have gained is also the man who can spend the child's fear.
N02.title: The Struck Name
N02.summary: Morrow Ludd removes Emrys Hask from the rite committee after a private audience, naming Hask's child in the new household order, and the seating order now has no friend on the committee. You bring the matter to Rurik Merrow in the tutor's study, where the treasury courtier accepts it because you let him ask Wren a question at lesson and the child answered without fear. Merrow now knows the child dreads the crown questions, and he will test that dread before the rite.
N02.image: the committee list with Hask's name struck out

N03.adapted: Five days remain. Linden Dunmore fixes the court's seating for the rite, placing Wren Tollen beside Morrow Ludd rather than before the crown, and the child's place is no longer a seat of answer but a seat of attendance. You trade the child's private fear to Rurik Merrow for his word to the steward, and the seating changes; the cost is that Wren learns his fear has been used, and Cadoc Ashgrove is called to the servants' hall to be questioned, so the servant who brought you the old questions is now marked by the palace for having helped you.
N03.title: The Moved Seat
N03.summary: Linden Dunmore fixes the court's seating for the rite, placing Wren Tollen beside Morrow Ludd rather than before the crown, and the child's place is no longer a seat of answer but a seat of attendance. You trade the child's private fear to Rurik Merrow for his word to the steward, and the seating changes. Wren learns his fear has been used, and Cadoc Ashgrove is called to the servants' hall to be questioned, so the servant who brought you the old questions is now marked by the palace for having helped you.
N03.image: the seating order rewritten, Wren's chair no longer before the crown

N04.adapted: Three days remain. Yestin Penhallow seals the coronation oath and places the crown in the rite chamber, and Cadoc Ashgrove leaves a folded copy of the oath's wording on your study desk by the window, where you find the marginal mark showing the chaplain changed the wording of the crown question. At the banquet in the great hall, Morrow Ludd raises a cup to the future of the realm while Wren watches from the tapestry gallery, and you answer by naming the child's hand on the crown; Linden Dunmore reads the decree again in the hall, Wren hears that his faltering is still the regent's way, and Brannoc Glaive steps back from you in the candlelight.
N04.title: The Sealed Oath
N04.summary: Three days remain, and Yestin Penhallow seals the coronation oath and places the crown in the rite chamber, while Cadoc Ashgrove leaves a folded copy of the oath's wording on your study desk by the window, where you find the chaplain's marginal mark changing the crown question. In the great hall, Morrow Ludd raises a cup to the future of the realm while Wren Tollen watches from the tapestry gallery, and you answer by naming the child's hand on the crown; Linden Dunmore reads the decree again in procedural absolutes, so Wren hears that his faltering is still the regent's way. Brannoc Glaive steps back from you in the candlelight, and the banquet ends with the oath sealed and the child's place still marked by attendance.
N04.image: the folded oath on your desk, its margin inked

N05.adapted: One day remains, and the rite chamber is set. The child's hand goes on the crown because Rurik Merrow and Brannoc Glaive stand in the rite chamber and Wren Tollen answers the first question in the old form; the crown is lifted, the regent's oath is not read in the altered wording, and the child learns what he has risked. Cadoc Ashgrove is dismissed from the servants' hall before the rite is done, and the child's trust is spent on the answer, so the crown is in his hand but the lesson book is closed to you.
N05.title: The Child's Hand
N05.summary: One day remains, and the rite chamber is set, so you bring Rurik Merrow and Brannoc Glaive to stand beside Wren Tollen while Yestin Penhallow leaves the sealed oath unread in its altered wording. Wren's hand goes on the crown and he answers the first question in the old form, learning what he has risked as Morrow Ludd watches the crown lifted without the regent's changed oath being spoken. Cadoc Ashgrove is dismissed from the servants' hall before the rite is done, and the child's trust is spent on the answer, leaving the crown in his hand and the lesson book closed to you.
N05.image: the child's hand resting on the crown before the rite chair

additions.text: Morrow Ludd offers Wren a named place in the new household order, behind Rurik Merrow's child, if Brannoc Glaive yields his seat in the rite chamber.

N06.adapted: The rite is over and the clock has taken nothing further. The child king sits before the crown with Rurik Merrow and Brannoc Glaive still in the chamber, but Cadoc Ashgrove is gone from the servants' hall and Emrys Hask has accepted the regent's household order; the realm keeps its child king, and you are left with a crown that is his and a trust that is no longer yours to spend.
N06.title: The Closed Lesson
N06.summary: The rite is over and the clock has taken nothing further. Wren Tollen sits before the crown with Rurik Merrow and Brannoc Glaive still in the chamber, while Cadoc Ashgrove is gone from the servants' hall and Emrys Hask has accepted the regent's household order. You are left with a crown that is his and a trust that is no longer yours to spend.
N06.image: the closed lesson book beside the child's crown

T2N01.adapted: Linden Dunmore reads the new household order in the great hall, naming Wren Tollen behind Rurik Merrow's child, and Yestin Penhallow sets the regent's crown on the rite chair. You let Wren say yes to his place before the order is written, so Cadoc Ashgrove stays at his place; Rurik Merrow takes the regent's seat in the new order, and Brannoc Glaive does not come back to the rite chamber.
T2N01.title: The Household Order
T2N01.summary: In the great hall, Linden Dunmore reads the new household order that names Wren Tollen behind the treasury courtier's child, and you let Wren say yes to his place before the order is written, so Cadoc Ashgrove stays at his place. In the rite chamber, Yestin Penhallow sets Morrow Ludd's crown on the rite chair, Rurik Merrow takes the regent's seat in the new order, and Brannoc Glaive's seat is left empty. Morrow's hand takes the crown at midsummer, and the child remains safe in the palace with his trust spent on survival.

T3N01.adapted: Yestin Penhallow seals the coronation oath and places the crown in the rite chamber, and Cadoc Ashgrove leaves a folded copy of the old wording on your study desk, where you find the marginal mark showing the chaplain changed the crown question. At the banquet in the great hall, Morrow Ludd raises a cup to the future of the realm while Wren watches from the tapestry gallery, and you answer by accepting the regent's future; Morrow names Wren's place in the new household order as the error seat, and Rurik Merrow's child is named before the child's own name, so the treasury courtier's cost is paid without the child's fear being spent.
T3N01.title: The Sealed Oath
T3N01.summary: Yestin Penhallow seals the coronation oath in the rite chamber, and Cadoc Ashgrove leaves a folded copy of the old wording on your study desk, where a marginal mark shows the chaplain changed the crown question. In the great hall, Morrow Ludd raises a cup to the realm's future while Wren Tollen watches from the tapestry gallery, and you answer by accepting that future. Morrow names Wren's place in the new household order as the error seat, with Rurik Merrow's child named before the child's own name, so the treasury courtier's cost is paid without the child's fear being spent.
T3N01.image: the folded old wording on the study desk, its margin inked

T3N02.adapted: At the rite chamber, the child's place is the error seat, and Yestin Penhallow is forced to read the old question aloud before the rite can continue. Wren Tollen answers the first question in the old form, and his hand goes on the crown; Rurik Merrow stands with him because the child's dread was not used as a public test, but Brannoc Glaive is no longer free to stand with him, because he is bound to the chaplain's double wording. You make Wren consent to his place before the rite is done, so Cadoc Ashgrove stays at the servants' hall.
T3N02.title: The Error Seat
T3N02.summary: In the rite chamber, Wren Tollen stands before the crown while Yestin Penhallow is forced to read the old question aloud because the double wording will not let the rite proceed on the altered one. Wren answers the first question in the old form and places his hand on the crown, and Rurik Merrow stands with him because the child's dread has not been made a public test. Brannoc Glaive is no longer free to stand with him, bound by the chaplain's double wording, and you make Wren consent to his place before the rite is done, so Cadoc Ashgrove stays at the servants' hall.
T3N02.image: the child's hand on the crown, the old question still in the chaplain's mouth

T3N03.adapted: The rite is over and the clock has taken nothing further. The child king sits before the crown with Rurik Merrow and Cadoc Ashgrove still in the palace, but Brannoc Glaive is gone from the rite chamber and Emrys Hask has accepted the regent's household order; the realm keeps its child king, and you are left with a crown that is his and a trust that is no longer yours to spend.
T3N03.title: What Is Left
T3N03.summary: The rite is over and the clock has taken nothing further. Wren Tollen sits before the crown with Rurik Merrow and Cadoc Ashgrove still in the palace, but Brannoc Glaive is gone from the rite chamber and Emrys Hask has accepted the regent's household order. The realm keeps its child king, and you are left with a crown that is his and a trust that is no longer yours to spend.
T3N03.image: the empty rite chamber after the crown has been laid, the door closed behind the court

C01.label: the regent's steward
C01.wants: the rite to proceed without incident so his household order is not questioned
C01.holds: the decree and the seating arrangements
C01.edge: arranges the seating to keep the child visible but powerless, believing this is a kindness
C01.tie: serves the regent who has appointed him to manage the rite
C01.voice: speaks in procedural absolutes that sound like benevolence: 'The chair is placed here for the child's comfort, not his command.'
C01.name: Linden Dunmore

C02.label: the aging servant
C02.wants: to see the child treated with the respect due to his name
C02.holds: memory of the child's mother and the old court's ways
C02.edge: remembers when the regent was a boy who feared the dark, and has not said so
C02.tie: has served the child since infancy and watches over him from the shadows
C02.voice: speaks in fragments of the past that answer the present: 'The queen did not kneel. She stood. You might try.'
C02.breaking_point: leaves the palace the day you let the child be moved without his consent
C02.name: Cadoc Ashgrove

C03.label: the seating courtier
C03.wants: to maintain their position in the court's hierarchy
C03.holds: the authority to arrange the physical space of the rite
C03.edge: removed from the committee to protect their child, and resents the regent's paternalism
C03.tie: owes the regent their current station but fears for their child's safety
C03.voice: measures the room in inches of dignity: 'If the child sits here, he is a guest. If he sits there, he is a prisoner. Choose.'
C03.breaking_point: turns against the regent if their child is moved again without warning
C03.name: Emrys Hask

C04.label: the child king
C04.wants: to be trusted with the questions and not made a fool
C04.holds: the crown's legitimacy and the court's expectation of his rule
C04.edge: wants to be a king but is terrified of the silence that follows his answers
C04.tie: trusts you as the only person who does not speak over him
C04.voice: asks questions that are not questions, seeking permission to exist: 'Is it true that if I say nothing, the crown stays with me?'
C04.breaking_point: stops listening to you the moment you correct his tone in front of the regent
C04.name: Wren Tollen

C05.label: the regent
C05.wants: to secure the realm by ruling it himself, believing the child is unfit
C05.holds: the crown council's decrees and the rite's machinery
C05.edge: genuinely believes he is saving the child from a burden he cannot bear
C05.tie: is the child's uncle and has raised him as a son, not a sovereign
C05.voice: speaks with the patience of a man who has already won: 'You are young. The realm is old. One must yield to the other.'
C05.name: Morrow Ludd

C06.label: the treasury courtier
C06.wants: to keep the realm's coffers full and the peace intact
C06.holds: the funds that pay for the rite and the court's loyalty
C06.edge: fears the child's independence more than the regent's control, as it threatens stability
C06.tie: serves the regent who guarantees their financial security
C06.voice: counts the cost of every gesture: 'A crown is expensive. A silence is cheaper. Which can you afford?'
C06.breaking_point: withdraws support if the child's rule leads to visible waste or debt
C06.name: Rurik Merrow

C07.label: the oath courtier
C07.wants: to ensure the rite's legal and spiritual validity
C07.holds: the sealed coronation oath and the ritual's form
C07.edge: believes the oath binds the regent more than the child, and fears the regent will break it
C07.tie: serves the regent who appointed them to oversee the oath
C07.voice: recites the rules as if they are prayers: 'The oath is ink. The ink is dry. The dry ink does not move.'
C07.breaking_point: opposes the regent if the oath is read incorrectly or altered
C07.name: Brannoc Glaive

C08.label: the regent's chaplain
C08.wants: to perform the rite with perfect liturgical accuracy
C08.holds: the sealed crown and the rite chamber's sanctity
C08.edge: fears that the child's failure will be seen as a divine rejection of the line
C08.tie: serves the regent who directs the spiritual tone of the court
C08.voice: speaks in the passive voice of the gods: 'It is done. It is set. It is not to be questioned.'
C08.name: Yestin Penhallow

plan.assessment: T1 answers the question with rightful rule: the child's hand goes on the crown, but the price is the child's easy trust, the aging servant, and the seating courtier. Missing worlds include the regent's coronation passing while the child is preserved under it, and a pole_a outcome where the aging servant is kept or the oath courtier is the one lost. The story can part early at N01, N02, or N03 through unused ways that change who holds the oath wording and what the child's fear costs.

seeds.motivation: When the regent offers the child a place in the new household order, you come to want the child kept safe under that order rather than risk him on the crown questions, because the chaplain has sealed the oath and the child's fear has already been spent in the hall.
seeds.strategy: Accept the regent's future at the banquet, trade the oath courtier's seat for the promise that the child will remain in the palace, and let the treasury courtier's child be named before the child so the household order can hold.
seeds.trigger: you traded the oath courtier's seat for the regent's promise that the child would remain in the palace

ending.title: The Safe Child
ending.summary: The regent's hand takes the crown at midsummer, and the child is named in the new household order behind the treasury courtier's child. The child remains safe in the palace, but his trust is spent on survival, and the oath courtier's seat is gone from the rite chamber.
ending.changed: the regent is crowned and the child is preserved under him

seeds.why_different: T1 keeps the child king and loses the aging servant; this line lets the regent take the crown and keeps the child safe under him, with the oath courtier and treasury courtier lost instead of standing.

seeds.motivation: When the seating order moves the child beside the regent, you come to want the child's fear kept private and the old oath wording made visible, because the child has just learned that his dread can be used as a bargaining piece.
seeds.strategy: Let the oath courtier carry the old oath wording to the regent's chaplain, keep the child's lesson from becoming a public test, and use the chaplain's double wording to force the rite back to the old question.
seeds.trigger: you let the oath courtier carry the old oath wording to the regent's chaplain

ending.title: The Error Seat
ending.summary: The child's place is moved to a seat that looks like an error, and the chaplain is forced to read the old question aloud before the rite can continue. The child's hand goes on the crown, but the oath courtier is no longer free to stand with him, and the aging servant stays at the servants' hall.
ending.changed: the chaplain holds both the old and the new wording, and the rite is saved by the error itself

seeds.why_different: T1 keeps the oath courtier and loses the aging servant; this line keeps the aging servant and loses the oath courtier, with the child's fear preserved private and the seating courtier still gone.

promises.reading: This is a high-stakes political thriller set in a single, suffocatingly elegant palace, where the weapon is not a sword but a whisper and the battlefield is the mind of a child. The audience wants to feel the precariousness of holding power together with glue and hope, knowing that the clock is ticking and the enemy is already winning.
promises.player_fantasy: To be the quiet, intelligent architect of a fragile defense, watching a beloved child grow up against the clock while the ground shifts under your feet.

promises.what: a private moment where the child king reveals a secret or fear that changes the tutor's strategy
promises.why: the core asset is the child's trust; the player must feel the weight of that intimacy

promises.what: a courtier who defects or is removed, forcing the player to re-evaluate their alliances
promises.why: the Kernel explicitly demands the ability to lose people, creating relational collapse

promises.what: a servant who slips a piece of crucial information, perhaps accidentally, perhaps as a gift
promises.why: the player has no soldiers; information is the only currency, and it must feel fragile and human

promises.what: the Regent's plan visibly advancing, such as a decree issued or a ritual prepared, regardless of the player's actions
promises.why: the Kernel states the plan advances on its own; the player must feel the inevitability of the threat

promises.what: a tense conversation where the Regent and the Tutor speak with courtesy but lethal intent
promises.why: the Regent is clever and patient; the conflict must be verbal and psychological, not physical

set_pieces.scene: the child king hiding in a tapestry room, listening to the Regent's speech through the fabric
a banquet where the Regent offers a toast to the 'future' that is clearly aimed at the Tutor's position
a servant being dismissed or punished in front of the Tutor, signaling the cost of loyalty
the Tutor finding a letter or symbol that proves the Regent's move is closer than expected

promises.tone_engine: Elegant and oblique: the danger is never shouted; it is implied in the arrangement of flowers, the pause before a reply, and the way a door is closed. Precarious dread: the player always feels one step away from ruin, and the loss of allies is felt as a physical blow.
obligatory_cast: a loyal but aging servant who remembers the Tutor's past and serves as a moral anchor
a courtier who is genuinely confused by the politics and may swing either way based on the Tutor's kindness
must_not: no open warfare or battle scenes: the conflict is resolved through politics, persuasion, and survival
no sudden, unearned loyalty: courtiers must have reasons to defect or stay, and their loss must feel earned by the narrative flow

otherwise: you traded the child's private fear to the treasury courtier for his word to the steward
you let Wren Tollen's hand go on the crown because Rurik Merrow and Brannoc Glaive stood in the rite chamber and the child answered the first question in the old form
